I've been deep in SEO for 15 years.

I know these 3 are the types of content you need: 

A lot of brands that come to us at Searchable are halfway there. 
Their content is technically fine, but it never gets recommended by AI.

The first thing we do is make sure they have their content mix in order.  
And that each type of content is doing its job. 

Because most folks are stuck at the top part, and ignore the rest... 
Their pages are crawlable, but are often never cited.

These are the 3 types that every brand needs and why they matter:   

1️⃣ Authority Pages
↳ For the people who don't yet know a solution like yours exists. 

They need clarity before they need a product. Your job is to become the source they trust before they enter the market, which means depth over volume. Educational guides, how-to content, frameworks, data-led posts. The content that gets cited is dense with real examples and first-hand experience.

2️⃣ Decision Pages
↳ For the people who understand the problem and are now weighing up their options.

When we built Searchable, instead of explaining how we help, we got founders to ask ChatGPT about their own sector and watch competitors show up above them. Be specific and honest, show who each option suits, where you're stronger, and where another solution might fit better. Buyers and AI both see through fake-neutral comparisons that only exist to promote you.

3️⃣ Money Pages
↳ For the people who already know they have a problem and are ready to act.

This is where the buying decision gets made. And it's increasingly where AI Overviews show up, which means the buying moment is now an AI moment. Give them clear answers, strong proof, pricing context, FAQs, and real reasons to trust you. When someone's ready to act, you’ll lose them FAST if they have to get through a 2,000-word blog to understand what you do.

Most of your customers won't move through the funnel in order. 

Someone might land on your pricing page straight from a Claude recommendation, 
Or they may read a case study with no context. 

Every page has to carry enough of the story to work on its own.

And don’t skimp on any part of the funnel, it only works when complete. 
Skip any stage, and you’ll have plenty of visibility with no conversions.

True story...
My 1st business: Failed. 
My 2nd business: Nearly destroyed by Covid.
My 3rd business: $35M raised, 100 people hired, #1 UK startup.
My 4th business: 7 successfully sold-out cohorts teaching personal brand. 
My 5th business: $85M valuation in 5 months.

It seems simple written down like that. 

But the real story is much more complicated. 

In 2009, I was 19, and my brother and I were trying to start our first company.

We spent 5 or 6 months and 10s of £1000s building a platform to help students find universities.

It gained some traction, but we had no idea how to raise or scale, so it went nowhere.

Then I went to uni and started working with startups, offering marketing in exchange for equity.

Most of them failed, and equity alone didn't pay my rent.

(A good lesson not to bet your income on other people's outcomes !)

So I built an agency and called it Adjust Media.

I did work for anyone and everyone, all the while doubting myself. 

But I kept thinking, "There are 10,000 agencies in the UK. I'm 21, I look like a child, and I'm less experienced than everyone I'm competing against." 

So I niched and became the digital marketing agency for luxury brands.

That was the origin of Verb Brands, a successful pivot.

Then COVID hit, and the business nearly got destroyed. 

Instead, I changed the model to retained revenue.

We then came out of Covid with a slightly bigger business, fully retained, and a valuation multiple that went from 6x profit to 11x.

I sold that for 8 figures at 30 years old.

After that, the wins started stacking up: 

- Lottie reached No. 1 start-up in the UK in 2025 
- The Creator Accelerator has 7 sold-out cohorts
- Searchable hit an $85M valuation in 5 months

But that was only because I spent a decade and a half building the wrong things and pushing through to find out what actually works. 

The point is that in business, consistency and persistence are what truly matter. 

You're never going to get it right the first time.

Businesses don't just pop up fully formed and error-free. 

You need to notice the flaws and adjust fast... 

Businesses are complex systems with moving parts that can break at any time. 

And with market changes and global trends shifting fast, 
Founders must see the big picture and make improvements accordingly. 

I personally do an audit across 8 key areas every quarter. 

Here are some leaks I caught and how I fixed them ⬇️
(Check out the sheet for more details !) 

1️⃣ Marketing and Personal Brand

❌ Post when you remember to, or only when you're launching something.
✅ Post daily on the platforms your buyers use, build your personal brand, and turn happy clients into case studies. 

2️⃣ Sales

❌ Treat sales as something you'll get to, and give away free calls to anyone who asks.
✅ Treat it as a profession with a weekly rhythm, and sell the transformation before the price.

3️⃣ AI Search and SEO

❌ Optimise for Google the way you did three years ago and hope you show up in AI search.
✅ Optimise for both at once, structure your content to be cited, and track exactly where you appear across ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini.

(Or, even better, have Searchable do that last part for you: https://lnkd.in/epgXyFmi !) 

4️⃣ Product

❌ Keep building features nobody asked for before you know anyone wants them.
✅ Ship the smallest version that delivers real value, then let customer feedback build the roadmap.

5️⃣ Team and Hiring

❌ Hire cheap and defensively, then spend your week managing people who need managing.
✅ Bring in A-players for specific problems. One is worth more than five B-players.

6️⃣ Systems and Delegation

❌ Let every lead, decision, and delivery run through you, and call that being busy.
✅ Protect your 20%, delegate 80%, and document it so the business isn't dependent on you.

7️⃣ Finances

❌ Chase revenue and never look at whether it's actually profit.
✅ Grow profit first, turn one-off work into recurring revenue, and build something that's sellable even if you never plan to sell.

8️⃣ Positioning

❌ Try to be for everyone, and end up competing with everyone.
✅ Niche down until you're the obvious choice, and say what you do and who for in one sentence.

If you want success in all 8 areas of your business, 
Start improving them before there’s a problem to fix. 

Better to make your business leak-proof from the start, 
Than waste time plugging holes later !

items.content:
Not long ago, ~6% of commercial Google searches returned AI Overviews. 

That figure is now above 90%, and no SEO is not dead...

I don't think anyone, including Google, expected it to move this fast.

We are witnessing the category get rewritten every week. 
It’s been a wild ride watching this play out in real time !

And it matters especially because of the type of searches these are. 

Low-intent, navigational queries rarely trigger an AI Overview. 
The ones that almost always do are commercial, high-intent searches. 

That's the exact moment a buyer is deciding about your brand or business,  
And whether they trust you enough to opt in. 

They can't trust you if they can't see you... 
And if your search strategy ignores AI search, they never will. 

So the traffic that you're losing now isn't random at all. 
That's all the traffic that was about to convert and didn't. 

But that doesn't mean SEO is dead. It means the moment worth optimising for has moved.

Google still handles over 13 billion searches a day. 
Most people are still searching the way they always have. 

But the foundations you built for SEO, structure, authority, clarity, are now what get you cited in the Overview too. 

AEO isn't a replacement for SEO. It's built on top of it. 
Ignore SEO and you've got nothing for AI to cite in the first place.

To explain as clearly as possible, these are the top 3 changes that should be on your radar:

1️⃣ The buying moment is now an AI moment.

For years the scoreboard was ranking position and clicks, and both still matter, but neither tells the full story once an Overview answers the query before the buyer reaches your page. 

Share of voice is the metric that's been added, how often you're the source being cited. Ranking gets you into the running for that citation, so this isn't ranking versus citation, it's ranking plus.

2️⃣ The erosion is landing where the money is.

At 6% presence, the Overview was a curiosity. Above 90%, it's where high-intent discovery happens. 

This isn't spread evenly across search either. Navigational queries rarely trigger an Overview, the commercial ones almost always do. 

Win the citation, and you take the intent your competitor was counting on.

3️⃣ The Overview is a channel of its own.

AI-referred traffic converts at around 2x standard organic. 

The buyer lands having already been given an answer, so you get fewer touches, higher intent, quicker decisions. Smaller volume, but it converts hard.

If you want to get out ahead of this, you're still on time. 
But you need an audit to know exactly where the gaps are.

It shows you where you need to start across the top 4 AI tools.

I’ve built 100+ teams across 4 8-figure businesses.

Here’s everything you need to build a high performing team: 

4 years into Verb, my first business, I had nearly 50 staff, and performance was… good. 

Unfortunately, my bar was set at exceptional. 

I had to replace 5 mid-level managers with 2 industry veterans, 
A tough (slightly more expensive) call that was more than worth it.  

In 1 year, they restructured operations, cut headcount, and lifted output by 30%.
For the first time, I wasn't needed in the day-to-day.

That's how I learned the real value of an A-player. 

Since then, I’ve gone through all the ups and downs of building great teams. 
And these are the 7 frameworks I always come back to. 

Here's a summary of each:
(See the visual for the full breakdown !)

1️⃣ The A-Player Formula

What it is: Commitment to hiring A-players. 
How to use it: Hire fewer, better people. 

2️⃣ The ALIGN Hiring Framework

A: Anchor the role to a real business outcome
L: Look for cognitive diversity
I: Institutionalise role clarity before they start
G: Generate the environment to onboard them properly
N: Nail the economic case for the hire

3️⃣ The SBI Feedback Model

S: Situation, when and where it happened
B: Behaviour, what you actually saw, no judgement
I: Impact, the effect it had

4️⃣ Radical Candor (Kim Scott)

What it is: Care personally and challenge directly. 
How to use it: Say the hard thing early and kindly, before it festers.

5️⃣ Freedom & Responsibility + the Keeper Test (Netflix)

What it is: Give people real freedom, hold a real bar, and pay top of market. 
How to use it: Trust people, stop hovering, and pay them enough. 

6️⃣ The Trust Triangle (Frances Frei, Harvard)

Authenticity: They're getting the real you
Logic: Your judgement stacks up
Empathy: They know you actually care

7️⃣ RAPID Decision-Making (Bain & Company)

R: Recommend, propose the plan
A: Agree, who has to sign off
P: Perform, who executes
I: Input, who informs the call
D: Decide, who makes the final call

And my top tip overall: hire for personality and passion first. 
You can teach skills on the job, but the right mindset is gold.  

We're building the Searchable team using these principles. 
And so far they've completely blown it out of the water. 

$85 million valuation and just getting started.

items.content:
I've hired 100s of people across 4 8-figure businesses.

My best hires did not have the most experience...

Scaling Verb Brands, I brought in people with big agency names. 
They had the impressive titles and strong references...

But time after time, those credentials let me down.

It took more than a few fumbles to learn that experience ≠ impact. 

Nearly any role can be taught with the right training and culture.
What I really needed to find was drive, hunger, and resilience. 

(The skills that can't be taught !)  

So I created a framework to bypass hiring mistakes and wasted time.

I call it ALIGN: 

A — Anchor the Role in Business Reality
↳ Every hire should tie to a strategic goal.
↳ Don't hire a marketing manager. Hire to increase qualified leads by 30%.

L — Look for Cognitive Diversity
↳ How someone processes a problem matters more than what they know.
↳ Pose a real scenario in the interview and watch how they solve it. 

I — Institutionalise Role Intelligence
↳ Most hiring failures come from unclear expectations.
↳ If you can't describe the function of the role, you're not ready to hire.

G — Generate the Right Environment
↳ Have the infrastructure ready before they arrive.
↳ Without it, you'll lose people before they've even really started.

N — Nail the Economic Case
↳ Every hire should pay for itself. Have their direct impact in mind.  
↳ This stops over-hiring and helps you say no to the wrong candidates.

Beyond the framework, there are 4 things I do in every interview:

1️⃣ Design questions around behaviour
↳ "Your top client is about to churn. You have 48 hours. Walk me through what you'd do."

This helps me see how they think, not just the answer they prepared. 

2️⃣ Look for pattern recognition and pace
↳ "What's a system you built or fixed in a past role, and how did you know it needed fixing?"

If they can't answer this one, they might not be used to taking initiative. 

3️⃣ Test for care
↳ Watch how they follow up. You can't fake it, and you can't train for it. 

A thoughtful note or reflection on the conversation goes a long way.

4️⃣ Hire for where the business is going
↳ Hiring reactively to fill a gap meant I replaced the role months later.

Now I hire someone who can grow into the business in 12 months.

An A-player will run circles around B-players any day. 

I learned that over more than a decade of hiring, 
But you can get out ahead of it with the framework above.

items.content:
Average founders think their product is the moat. 

The best founders know it isn't. The story is...

Because your product can be copied. 
Someone with deeper pockets can build the same thing, and probably better.

What they can't copy:

- Your story
- Your insight
- Your audience who already trust you...

That's where I think the real moat is in 2026 and beyond.

I've launched 3 companies and each one was easier than the last.

Not necessarily because the products I built got better.
In my opinion, it was because of the audience I built.

I had people follow along with my story, and they got involved with each new business.

When I started Verb, I had nothing. Every client call started cold.
By Searchable, founders showed up already sold on what we do. 

They'd watched hours of my content before we ever spoke.

Narrative and storytelling are assets that compound over time.

These 6 frameworks are some of the ones I've leaned on to build them:

1️⃣ Hero's Journey

A common adventure arc that mirrors every great story.
Useful for: Pitch decks, brand messaging, and customer case studies.

2️⃣ The Golden Circle

Lead with why you exist rather than what you sell.
Useful for: Investor pitches, team alignment and brand positioning. 

3️⃣ What, So What, Now What

Turn boring facts into a reason to act.

What = The fact.
So What = Why it matters.
Now What = What to do about it.

Useful for: All-hands meetings, investor updates and board meetings. 

4️⃣ Freytag's Pyramid

Narrative arc that shows struggle, breakthrough, and resolution.
Useful for: Any content that wants to emphasise emotion.

5️⃣ The Origin Story Framework

Every founder has a story. 
Structure it like this:

Before = The problem you faced.
Turning Point = The moment everything changed.
After = The mission you're now on.

Useful for: Intros, investor pitches, and rallying your team.

6️⃣ Pixar's Story Framework

Mirrors classic narrative arcs used in every Pixar film.
Useful for: Any narrative that needs structure and flow.

Ultimately, storytelling is how you turn attention into trust you can monetise.

Leverage it for content, marketing, and beyond. It's worth it.

items.content:
Both under-planning AND over-planning kill businesses.

Success lies in mastering 3 types of plans 👇

Founders love to hide behind over-planning because it feels productive.  
But “refining strategy” is not a good use of an entire quarter ! 

Planning can also keep you from the clarity that comes with taking action and adjusting. 

To be clear, I’m not saying “plan less”...
But I am saying “plan smarter.” 

While building my first business, Verb Brands (Adjust Media at the time), 
I had loads of ambition and passion, but no real structure. 

I knew roughly where I wanted to go, and we did move forward, 
But we were all over the road with no clear direction. 

This is how I wish I had been taught to plan my business back then 👇

🔭 Strategic Planning

This is where you decide what the business is actually trying to become. You need to look at the bigger picture, around 3-5 years out, and create specific goals.  

The hardest part of strategic planning is deciding what you won't do. Clarifying the direction and being specific will help you know when to say yes and when to step away. 

Review your strategy annually to make sure you’re on track ! 

📋 Tactical Planning

This is where strategy becomes projects the team can actually execute. Tactical planning bridges the gap between the vision and the daily work. 

You’ll need to allocate resources properly at this stage. 

The most common mistake here is spending 3 months planning and 1 month executing. You want to do the exact opposite. 

You really want to plan 1 to 3 years out and break deadlines down into quarterly milestones.

⚡ Operational Planning

This is your daily and weekly planning that will get adjusted most often. You’ll probably revisit this plan every week. 

Even with a brilliant strategy and a solid quarter mapped out, things can start to fall apart if you don’t have tangible operational plans. 

Keep your KPIs realistic here; there’s nothing less productive than overloading your team with unrealistic expectations. That’s where frequent adjustments can help. 

Nothing slows momentum like building with unclear intent.

And this 3-tier breakdown is by far the best way to clarify where you’re business is headed. 

The layers feed into each other, so you can’t realistically skimp on any of them. 

✅ Strategic planning is your destination. 
✅ Tactical planning maps the route. 
✅ Operational planning is how you actually drive.

A business is a complex ecosystem and there are 1000s of factors to success.

But proper planning is how good businesses become excellent.

items.content:
Winning the first 10 customers at my first business took months. 

For Searchable, we did it within 24 hours. 

When I launched Verb at 21, I was basically starting from scratch. 
I had to prove myself and my business on every call. 

By the time I started Lottie, I'd been posting on LinkedIn for 18 months.
I started getting on calls with people who already knew who I was. 

With Searchable, I'd been building in public for 4 years.
Founders turned up pre-sold, having read or watched our content.

Each launch was easier than the last because all that work compounded. 
But it never would have started without those first 10 (hard-won) customers.

Here's the playbook I wish I'd had at the beginning 👇

1️⃣ Get painfully specific

Define your ideal customer profile before you build anything, then use it as a filter for every decision.

Verb went from "marketing agency" to "digital marketing agency for luxury brands." We went from competing with 10,000 agencies to being the only obvious choice in our category.

2️⃣ Talk to 10 real people

Find 10 people who fit your ICP and listen, don't pitch.

Ask what they're struggling with, what they've tried, and why it didn't work.

3️⃣ Nail your positioning in one sentence

[What you do] + [Who you do it for]

For example: Searchable is an autonomous SEO, AEO, and GEO Growth Engineer for marketing teams.
(Shameless plug, but I’ll drop the link here for anyone interested: https://lnkd.in/epgXyFmi) 

4️⃣ Build one tiny feature

Strip it to the one thing customers actually want and get feedback. (No more than 2 weeks !)

When we built Searchable, we asked: What's the single thing we can build right now that proves this works? The answer was prompt tracking. 

5️⃣ Do free work to earn your first case study

A named case study with a verifiable result beats content alone. 

Pick one ideal client and deliver something brilliant for free. Make sure others can click and confirm it as well.  

6️⃣ Turn content viewers into customers

Post consistently so your ICP sees you. Reach out personally, engaging but not enquiring.

Most people who see your content never come inbound. Go and get them.

7️⃣ Make those first 10 obsessed

Over-deliver and follow up. Let word of mouth carry you to customers 11, 12, 13.

When we opened Searchable to early access users, I spent 10 hours a day on calls with them while the team built through the night.

It compounds slowly at first, but patience is key. 
Once it takes off, it takes off for good.

items.content:
Even the smallest choices impact your long-term success. 

World-class founders know this better than ANYONE.  

Genuinely, if you want to master or build anything, 
You cannot leave your progress up to willpower alone. 

Habits become a routine, and a routine becomes an identity.
Eventually, being a high-performer just becomes who you are.

If I had to list the top 12 I see in the top 1% founders, this would be it:

➡️ Systemise everything 

You can only go so far with sheer willpower alone. Instead, build systems. Anything I do more than twice I turn into a checklist or a template for it.

➡️ Protect your zone of genius

There is a small set of work that only you can do and will actually help you scale. Find your top 3 tasks and protect them at all costs.

➡️ Run a monthly 80/20 audit

Once a month, go through your calendar, the month behind you and month ahead of you. Then, mark the 20% of tasks that drove the most results. 

➡️ Eat the frog

I do the hardest task of the day first, before other priorities land on my plate. Decide tonight what your frog is, then eat it before you open your inbox.

➡️ Turn your phone off for deep work

It goes off and into another room. The jump in quality of work when it's out of reach is something you have to feel for yourself to believe. Try doing that yourself in your next deep work block.

➡️ Set delegation triggers

I don't decide what to hand off in the moment, I set rules that decide for me... Write 2 or 3 delegation rules of your own and hold yourself to them.

➡️ Build your calendar around energy

I build my week around when I'm at my best for a given type of work. Map your own energy for a week, then move your hardest work into your peak window.

➡️ Write tomorrow's top 3 each evening

I set my priorities when I'm calm, so I'm not picking them when I'm tired and reactive first thing. 

➡️ Close open loops ASAP

Open-ended tasks can stay in your mind for a very long time. Give every task on your list a date today.

➡️ Set deadlines on everything

The moment a task has a hard finish line, it gets done properly and on time.

➡️ Review your numbers daily

You can't fix what you're not watching. Pick your core metrics and put them somewhere you'll see them daily.

➡️ Move your body every day

Even if it's only 20 minutes, it doesn't have to be extreme. But movement is good for your body AND mind. 

You won't find quick fixes here, because that doesn't build routines. 
Habits are unglamorous and often boring, but they work. 

That’s how I’ve built 4 8-figure businesses, 
While still showing up for myself and the people I love.
